newsitem.title: UK: Diesel vehicle sales to rebound in Europe - Daiwa.
newsitem.headline: Diesel vehicle sales to rebound in Europe - Daiwa.

text.p: European sales of diesel vehicles will rebound in the next few years after stagnating in 1995 and 1996 due to growing environmental concerns, the Daiwa Institute of Research said on Wednesday.
"We estimate that diesel car penetration in Europe will increase steadily over the next 10 years and could reach over 35 percent by 2005," Daiwa said.
"By then, the diesel market will have sales of over four million units, which is nearly 60 percent higher than in 1996," it said.

Daiwa said diesel sales had suffered a setback in the last two years after a period of rapid growth as drivers became concerned about the polluting affects of diesel exhaust and the health risk posed by soot particles.

In France, which has the highest percentage of diesel cars, market share declined to just over 39 percent in 1996 from a peak of 47 percent in 1994. Britain also saw significantly slower sales as diesel's share fell to 17 percent from 22 percent.

Environmental pressures aside, diesel car sellers like PSA Peugeot, Renault, Mercedes and Volkswagen had to struggle with French incentives to buy smaller vehicles, where the case for diesel is less compelling, higher duties in Britain, and higher rates of registration tax in Germany, Italy and the Netherlands.

But with exhaust emissions falling after the Europe-wide introduction of low-sulphur fuel last autumn, tax breaks for ultra-clean diesel and improved performance from diesel-powered engines, the outlook is improving, Daiwa said.

"Between now and the end of the century, the recovery of diesel's advantage (over gasoline) should come from the more widespread marketing of direct injection turbo diesels and from the recent changes in the measurement of fuel consumption," it said.
Daiwa said greater emphasis on urban driving in new fuel consumption measurements would favour conventional diesels over petrol cars.
In addition, a current surplus of gasoline and a shortage of diesel in Europe should, perversely, benefit the diesel car market in the longer term, it said.
"The two options that are open to oil companies are to increase diesel capacity...or just cut refining capacity across the board," Daiwa said.

"A switch to more diesel capacity is bound to lead to a short period of oversupply and hence cheaper diesel prices, or if a straight capacity cut is sanctioned then the resulting higher prices for fuel...will make customers focus more on fuel efficiency of engine types - again to the benefit of direct injection diesel."
